purpose: Test two stated workshop requirements separately, then follow their truth values through a chosen logical connective.
meaning: A truth-functional connective determines a compound statement from the truth values of its parts. AND requires both statements; inclusive OR requires at least one. The material conditional fails only when its antecedent is true and its consequent false. A truth table makes every allowed input combination explicit.

definition.setting: Classical two-valued propositional logic realized by two inclusive dimension tests on one panel.
definition.formal_latex: P:x\ge6\,\mathrm{cm},\quad Q:y\ge4\,\mathrm{cm};\quad P\land Q,\ P\lor Q,\ P\to Q,\ P\leftrightarrow Q,\ \neg P.
conditions: Panel length x and width y are real centimetre measurements from zero to twelve. P means x≥6 cm and Q means y≥4 cm, with equality included.
Use classical True/False truth values. Inclusive OR is true when either or both inputs are true; AND is true only when both are true.
P→Q is false exactly for P true and Q false. P↔Q is true when the two truth values agree. ¬P reverses P and ignores Q.
The material conditional states a truth-table relation; it does not by itself express causation, relevance, a promise or the full meaning of an ordinary-language conditional.
definition.domain_notes: The numeric dimension domain supplies concrete statements. Truth values change at thresholds; smooth movement of a panel does not create a partly true statement.
definition.proof_status: Definition-level sources and original restricted-family arguments; independent review pending.

prompts.prompt: Why can P→Q be true when P is false?
prompts.answer: Only a true antecedent with a false consequent violates the material truth-table condition; no causal relation is asserted.

prompts.prompt: Does a panel halfway to the threshold make P partly true?
prompts.answer: No. In this classical model the measurement moves continuously, while the inclusive threshold test has a definite truth value.
